claim: Early Vangl2 deletion leads to partial corpus callosum and hippocampal commissure agenesis in Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO conditional mutants.
source: To evaluate the impact of Vangl2 deletion in the forebrain, we generated Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO conditional mutants, efficiently deleting Vangl2 in the early dorsal telencephalon (Vangl2 cKO mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing agenesis of corpus callosum and hippocampal commissure in the mutant mice, as described in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Vangl2 expression was significantly decreased in the telencephalon as early as E13.5, including the hippocampus and cortex, in Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO mice.
source: As expected, Vangl2 expression did not vary in the cerebellum or spinal cord, where Emx1 is not expressed, but was significantly decreased in the telencephalon as early as E13.5, including the hippocampus and cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: No significant disruption of the internal capsule fibers was observed at early stages (E13.5) in Vangl2 cKO mice.
source: In these early stages, we did not observe a significant disruption of the internal capsule fibers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by neurofilament and DAPI staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Analysis of brain sections from Vangl2 cKO mice confirmed the agenesis of both the corpus callosum and the hippocampal commissure in the dorso-caudal region of the forebrain.
source: Analysis of brain sections from Vangl2 cKO mice confirmed the agenesis of both the corpus callosum (cc, magenta outline) and the hippocampal commissure (hc, cyan outline) in the dorso-caudal region of the forebrain, while other major commissures appeared intact, as previously reported (Qu et al., 2014) (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining and histological data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E, and is also supported by citation to Qu et al., 2014.

claim: In control mice, commissural colossal and hippocampal fibers cross the cerebral midline, while in Vangl2 cKO mice they did not.
source: To further validate the hc deficit, we injected AAV9 viruses coding for GFP in the CA3 region of the hippocampus and processed the brain 4 weeks later. The results showed that in control mice, commissural colossal and hippocampal fibers cross the cerebral midline, while in Vangl2 cKO mice they did not (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by AAV-GFP injection experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The observed deficit in corpus callosum was not due to a decrease in upper-layer neurons, as the thickness of the somato-sensory region of the cortex, the number of Cux1-positive neurons, and the thickness of the layer they define were unchanged between controls and Vangl2 cKO.
source: The observed deficit in cc was not due to a decrease in upper-layer neurons, as the thickness of the somato-sensory region of the cortex, or the number of Cux1-positive neurons and the thickness of the layer they define, were unchanged between controls and Vangl2 cKO (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data of cortical thickness and Cux1-positive neurons shown in Figure 1E–G.

claim: Vangl2 is present in neuronal growth cones at 2 days in vitro (DIV2) in relation to F-actin distribution.
source: Immunofluorescence labeling of cultured hippocampal neurons showed the presence of Vangl2 (magenta) in neuronal growth cones at 2 days in vitro (DIV2) in relation to F-actin distribution (phalloidin staining, blue) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Vangl2 protein appeared in the form of puncta, which were located along filopodia, close to the center of the growth cones, and along the growing neurite shafts.
source: Vangl2 protein appeared in the form of puncta, which were located along filopodia (yellow asterisks), close to the center of the growth cones (red asterisk), and along the growing neurite shafts (green arrowhead), but also exhibited some degree of diffuse staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Vangl2 cKO neurons, most of the Vangl2 staining disappeared, cross-validating the antibody specificity and the efficiency of Vangl2 deletion.
source: In Vangl2 cKO neurons, most of the staining disappeared (Figure 2A), cross-validating the antibody specificity and the efficiency of Vangl2 deletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The absence of Vangl2 affected growth cone morphology, with Vangl2 cKO growth cones exhibiting more fusiform-shaped growth cones than controls.
source: We noticed that the absence of Vangl2 affected growth cone morphology (Figure 2A–C). To quantify this effect, we defined a normalized shape index (S.I.), where values close to one represent circular objects and values close to zero represent elongated ones (Figure 2B). S.I. values were significantly smaller in the growth cones of Vangl2 cKO mice than in those of controls, confirming that the former group exhibits more fusiform-shaped growth cones than the latter group.
evidence: The claim is supported by shape index analysis shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The average area of the growth cones was unchanged between controls and Vangl2 cKOs.
source: The average area of the growth cones, however, was unchanged between controls and Vangl2 cKOs (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Growth cones from Vangl2 cKO mice plated on Ncad-Fc covered a longer distance and migrated faster than controls (+73%) within a 45 min observation period.
source: On average, within a 45 min observation period, growth cones from Vangl2 cKO mice plated on Ncad-Fc covered a longer distance (Figure 3A, dotted pink line, see also Videos 1 and 2) and migrated faster than controls (+73%, Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse DIC microscopy data shown in Figure 3A,B and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The growth cones of Vangl2 cKO neurons paused less in total and had a shorter average time per pause than controls.
source: The growth cones of Vangl2 cKO neurons paused less in total (Figure 3C) and had a shorter average time per pause than controls (Figure 3D), but the velocity between pauses was also higher than that of control growth cones (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C,D,E.

claim: No significant difference in growth cone movement was found between Vangl2 cKO and control neurons on laminin or PLL substrates.
source: We found no significant difference in growth cone movement between Vangl2 cKO and control neurons on laminin or PLL (Figure 3G,J,K), and no difference in the total time spent pausing was observed on laminin-coated substrates (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3G,H,J,K.

claim: Vangl2 deletion causes a selective enhancement of growth cone velocity which is dependent on N-cadherin adhesion.
source: Altogether, these results show that Vangl2 deletion causes a selective enhancement of growth cone velocity which is dependent on N-cadherin adhesion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing increased velocity on N-cadherin substrates but not on laminin or PLL substrates.

claim: The addition of either Netrin-1 or Wnt5 led to a significant increase in axonal length in both control and Vangl2 cKO neurons, and this increase was comparable between genotypes.
source: The addition of either Netrin-1 or Wnt5 led to a significant increase in axonal length in both control and Vangl2 cKO neurons, and this increase was comparable between genotypes (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by axonal length measurements shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Neuronal outgrowth in response to guidance cues is not affected by the absence of Vangl2.
source: This demonstrates that neuronal outgrowth in response to guidance cues is not affected by the absence of Vangl2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing comparable increases in axonal length in response to Netrin-1 or Wnt5 in both control and Vangl2 cKO neurons.

claim: In the absence of Vangl2, neurons presented a shift from more directed actin trajectories towards less diffuse/more confined trajectories when compared with controls.
source: On Ncad-Fc substrates, the variety of actin-mEos2 dynamics was highlighted by plotting the distribution of α coefficients obtained for control and Vangl2 cKO neurons (Figure 4B,C, compare also with PLL substrate in Figure 4—figure supplement 2K). In the absence of Vangl2, neurons presented a shift from more directed actin trajectories (higher α values) towards less diffuse/more confined trajectories (lower α values) when compared with controls (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sptPALM data showing the distribution of α coefficients in Figure 4B,C,D.

claim: The velocity of actin-mEos2 molecules within actin filaments was, on average, 23% slower in the growth cones of Vangl2 cKO neurons than in control growth cones.
source: Measurements restricted to directed trajectories (i.e. α ≥1.5) showed that the velocity of actin-mEos2 molecules within actin filaments was, on average, 23% slower in the growth cones of Vangl2 cKO neurons than in control growth cones (Figure 4E), suggesting that in the absence of Vangl2, the speed of retrograde actin flow in growth cones slowed down.
evidence: The claim is supported by sptPALM data showing actin flow velocity in Figure 4E.

claim: There was no global deficit in actin polymerization levels, as assessed by a similar ratio of F- to G-actin (F/G) in neurons with and without Vangl2.
source: This hypothesis was supported by the absence of a global deficit in actin polymerization levels, as assessed by a similar ratio of F- to G-actin (F/G) in neurons with and without Vangl2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2L).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing F/G actin ratios in Figure 4—figure supplement 2L.

claim: Microtubule dynamics was unaffected in the growth cones of Vangl2 cKO neurons, as assessed by tracking the movement of EB3-GFP comets.
source: Microtubule dynamics, which is also important for neuronal outgrowth and guidance, was unaffected in the growth cones of Vangl2 cKO neurons, as assessed by tracking the movement of EB3-GFP comets (Figure 4F,G, Videos 6 and 7), suggesting that Vangl2 primarily affects F-actin dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by EB3-GFP tracking data shown in Figure 4F,G and Videos 6 and 7.

claim: The observed shift towards smaller α values in Vangl2 cKO neurons suggests that the absence of this PCP protein leads to an increase in the coupling strength between the actin flow and adhesion molecules, thereby reducing the actin flow rate and increasing the migration speed.
source: The observed shift towards smaller α values in Vangl2 cKO neurons (Figure 4C,D) suggests that the absence of this PCP protein leads to an increase in the coupling strength between the actin flow and adhesion molecules, thereby reducing the actin flow rate and increasing the migration speed.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the sptPALM data and computer simulations showing the relationship between α values, coupling strength, and actin flow velocity.

claim: No differences were found in the levels of N-cadherin or β-catenin expression in hippocampi from controls and Vangl2 cKO mice.
source: We did not find differences in the levels of N-cadherin or β-catenin expression in hippocampi from controls and Vangl2 cKO mice, suggesting that Vangl2 deletion does not affect the global expression of the N-cadherin/catenin complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of Vangl2, there was an increased fraction of slow Ncad-GFP molecules at the membrane (+14%) or an extended turnover time of Ncad-GFP molecules engaged in homophilic bonds.
source: At the end of the second phase, which had much slower dynamics (~200 s), control neurons recovered up to 68% of their fluorescence, while Vangl2 cKO growth cones recovered only to 54%. Therefore, in the absence of Vangl2, there was an increased fraction of slow Ncad-GFP molecules at the membrane (+14%) or an extended turnover time of Ncad-GFP molecules engaged in homophilic bonds (Bard et al., 2008; Garcia et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data and is also supported by citations to Bard et al., 2008 and Garcia et al., 2015.

claim: The FRAP data were fitted with a diffusion/reaction model, from which an 83% decrease in the long-term turnover rate of N-cadherin adhesions in the absence of Vangl2 was extracted.
source: The FRAP data were fitted with a diffusion/reaction model, from which we extracted an 83% decrease in the long-term turnover rate of N-cadherin adhesions in the absence of Vangl2, supporting our hypothesis (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the absence of Vangl2, a significant fraction of N-cadherin with low mobility or stable anchoring is available for engagement in the clutch mechanism.
source: These results suggest that, in the absence of Vangl2, a significant fraction of N-cadherin with low mobility or stable anchoring is available for engagement in the clutch mechanism.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FRAP data showing decreased turnover rate of N-cadherin in Vangl2 cKO neurons.

claim: A comparison of the distribution of diffusion coefficients between genotypes showed a significant decrease in the proportion of fast-diffusing N-cadherin molecules in the absence of Vangl2, concomitant with a decrease in the fraction of confined molecules.
source: The median diffusion coefficient of Ncad-mEos2 molecules was not different in growth cones from Vangl2 cKO origin compared to controls (p=0.08) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). However, a comparison of the distribution of diffusion coefficients between genotypes showed a significant decrease in the proportion of fast-diffusing N-cadherin molecules in the absence of Vangl2, concomitant with a decrease in the fraction of confined molecules (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sptPALM data showing the distribution of diffusion coefficients in Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A plot of the MSD of Ncad-mEos2 molecules over time confirmed a global reduction in N-cadherin diffusion and covered area in the absence of Vangl2, with a sharp decrease after ~200 ms.
source: A plot of the MSD of Ncad-mEos2 molecules over time confirmed a global reduction in N-cadherin diffusion and covered area in the absence of Vangl2, with a sharp decrease after ~200 ms (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The strongest difference observed was a significant increase (+100%) in the density of domains per unit area (domains*µm-²) in Vangl2 cKO neurons.
source: The strongest difference observed was a significant increase (+100%) in the density of domains per unit area (domains*µm-²) in Vangl2 cKO neurons (Figure 6F), confirmed by the frequency distribution of nanodomain density (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: In the absence of Vangl2, N-cadherin turnover and the number of fast-diffusing N-cadherin molecules at the membrane decrease, while the number of confined molecules increases.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that in the absence of Vangl2, N-cadherin turnover and the number of fast-diffusing N-cadherin molecules at the membrane decrease, while the number of confined molecules increases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined sptPALM and FRAP data showing changes in N-cadherin dynamics in Vangl2 cKO neurons.

claim: These results are consistent with the formation of trans-dimers of N-cadherin and/or an increased local engagement of N-cadherin with F-actin.
source: These results are consistent with the formation of trans-dimers of N-cadherin and/or an increased local engagement of N-cadherin with F-actin.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the data on N-cadherin dynamics.

claim: No significant difference was observed in the global median diffusion coefficient of Vangl2 molecules whether the neurons were grown on Ncad-Fc- or laminin-coated substrates.
source: We observed no significant difference in the global median diffusion coefficient of Vangl2 molecules whether the neurons were grown on Ncad-Fc- or laminin-coated substrates (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A small decrease in Vangl2 diffusion at the periphery was observed on both substrates.
source: When we sorted the trajectories to compare the diffusion coefficients between the periphery and the center of the growth cones, we observed a small decrease in Vangl2 diffusion at the periphery on both substrates (Figure 7E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 7E,G.

claim: Plots of the MSDs of mEos2-Vangl2 molecules over time show a clear reduction in the area covered by Vangl2 molecules at the periphery on both substrates, with a more pronounced difference on Ncad-Fc than on laminin.
source: Plots of the MSDs of mEos2-Vangl2 molecules over time show a clear reduction in the area covered by Vangl2 molecules at the periphery on both substrates, with a more pronounced difference on Ncad-Fc than on laminin (Figure 7F,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 7F,H.

claim: The density of Vangl2 domains was higher on Ncad-Fc substrate than on laminin.
source: The density of Vangl2 domains was higher on Ncad-Fc substrate than on laminin (Figure 7K,L), a difference that can be explained by the larger surface area of the growth cones grown on laminin-coated substrates (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7K,L.

claim: A significant increase (+41%) in the ratio of mEos2-Vangl2 domains at the periphery vs the entire growth cone was observed on Ncad-Fc substrates compared to laminin substrates.
source: When we calculated the ratio of mEos2-Vangl2 domains at the periphery vs the entire growth cone, we observed a significant increase (+41%) in this ratio on Ncad-Fc substrates compared to laminin substrates (Figure 7M).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7M.

claim: N-cadherin interacting in trans can affect the distribution of Vangl2 molecules.
source: These data suggest that N-cadherin interacting in trans can affect the distribution of Vangl2 molecules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing differential distribution of Vangl2 on N-cadherin vs laminin substrates.

claim: Ncad-Fc-coated beads placed on Vangl2 cKO growth cones escaped the optical trap earlier than beads on control growth cones after 1 min, but also traveled longer distances.
source: Ncad-Fc-coated beads placed on Vangl2 cKO growth cones escaped the optical trap earlier than beads on control growth cones after 1 min, but also traveled longer distances (Figure 8A,B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by optical tweezers experiments shown in Figure 8A,B,D.

claim: The absence of Vangl2 did not affect the bead velocity after escaping the trap.
source: Importantly, the absence of Vangl2 did not affect the bead velocity after escaping the trap (Figure 8A,B,C), indicating that the actin flow is altered only when N-cadherin adhesions are engaged.
evidence: The claim is supported by optical tweezers experiments shown in Figure 8A,B,C.

claim: The escape probability of beads is significantly increased (+20%) when beads are placed on top of Vangl2 cKO growth cones.
source: Finally, we measured the escape probability of beads as described previously (Bard et al., 2008), and found that this index is significantly increased (+20%) when beads are placed on top of Vangl2 cKO growth cones (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by optical tweezers experiments shown in Figure 8E and is also supported by citation to Bard et al., 2008.

claim: The absence of Vangl2 increases the coupling efficiency between N-cadherin adhesions and the actin flow, thereby influencing the speed of actin flow and, ultimately, the displacement of growth cones.
source: These data support the model that the absence of Vangl2 increases the coupling efficiency between N-cadherin adhesions and the actin flow, thereby influencing the speed of actin flow and, ultimately, the displacement of growth cones.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined optical tweezers, sptPALM, and growth cone velocity data.

claim: The absence of Vangl2 in young neurons increases the migration rate of the neuronal growth cone, due to a reduced turnover of N-cadherin adhesions resulting in an increased mechanical connection to the actin retrograde flow.
source: Our study shows that the absence of Vangl2 in young neurons increases the migration rate of the neuronal growth cone, due to a reduced turnover of N-cadherin adhesions resulting in an increased mechanical connection to the actin retrograde flow.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by multiple experimental approaches including FRAP, sptPALM, and optical tweezers.

claim: Endogenous Vangl2 acts as a negative regulator of a molecular clutch between N-cadherin adhesions and F-actin in growth cones.
source: Collectively, these observations support a model in which endogenous Vangl2 acts as a negative regulator of a molecular clutch between N-cadherin adhesions and F-actin in growth cones (Model, Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the combined experimental data and is illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The inactivation of core PCP genes Celsr3 and Fzd3 leads to severe defects in multiple major axon tracts of the central nervous system.
source: It is well established that the inactivation of core PCP genes Celsr3 and Fzd3 leads to severe defects in multiple major axon tracts of the central nervous system (Feng et al., 2012; Hamblet et al., 2002; Hua et al., 2014; Tissir and Goffinet, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feng et al., 2012; Hamblet et al., 2002; Hua et al., 2014; Tissir and Goffinet, 2013.

claim: Neither Celsr3 nor Fzd3 deletion affect axonal outgrowth but rather disrupt the ability of the growth cones to respond to guidance cues.
source: It was further shown that neither Celsr3 nor Fzd3 deletion affect axonal outgrowth but rather disrupt the ability of the growth cones to respond to guidance cues (Chai et al., 2014; Hamblet et al., 2002; Hua et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chai et al., 2014; Hamblet et al., 2002; Hua et al., 2014.

claim: The inactivation of Vangl2 affects neural outgrowth, and more specifically, the outgrowth of Vangl2 cKO hippocampal neurons is sensitive to N-cadherin-mediated adhesion.
source: In contrast, we show here that the inactivation of Vangl2 affects neural outgrowth, and more specifically, that the outgrowth of Vangl2 cKO hippocampal neurons is sensitive to N-cadherin-mediated adhesion.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing increased growth cone velocity on N-cadherin substrates but not on laminin or PLL substrates.

claim: Core PCP genes do not use a conserved signaling cassette in young neurons as they do in epithelial cells, at least for axon guidance, and can activate specific signaling pathways independent from each other.
source: These results suggest that core PCP genes do not use a conserved signaling cassette in young neurons as they do in epithelial cells, at least for axon guidance, and can activate specific signaling pathways independent from each other (Guo et al., 2004; Klein and Mlodzik, 2004).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differences in phenotypes between Vangl2, Celsr3, and Fzd3 mutants, and is also supported by citations to Guo et al., 2004 and Klein and Mlodzik, 2004.

claim: Vangl2 participates in dynamic junctional remodeling, allowing hippocampal neurons to adapt to the environment encountered while navigating.
source: Our data strongly suggest that Vangl2 participates in this dynamic junctional remodeling role, allowing the hippocampal neurons to adapt to the environment encountered while navigating.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing Vangl2's role in regulating N-cadherin dynamics and growth cone velocity.

claim: Hippocampal and motor neurons may respond differently to defects in Vangl2 signaling.
source: In contrast, our results in hippocampal neurons show that neurite outgrowth is increased in the absence of Vangl2 but that Wnt5a-stimuated axonal outgrowth is not affected in Vangl2 cKO neurons. We may envision that hippocampal and motor neurons respond differently to defects in Vangl2 signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of results in hippocampal neurons with those reported by Shafer et al. in motor neurons.

claim: Vangl2 is a regulator of endocytosis in the context of junctional remodeling during tissue growth, including cell movement.
source: At a molecular level, it is tempting to conclude that Vangl2 is a regulator of endocytosis in the context of junctional remodeling during tissue growth, including cell movement.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on the data and literature on Vangl2's interactions with various proteins.

claim: There is accumulating evidence in various species and tissues that E-cadherin and N-cadherin turnover is modulated by Vangl2 and its orthologues, through direct or indirect interaction.
source: Within these interactors, there is now accumulating evidence in various species and tissues that E-cadherin and N-cadherin turnover is modulated by Vangl2 and its orthologues, through direct or indirect interaction (Classen et al., 2005; Warrington et al., 2013; Nagaoka et al., 2014a; Nagaoka et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Classen et al., 2005; Warrington et al., 2013; Nagaoka et al., 2014a; Nagaoka et al., 2014b.

claim: Vangl2 has been shown to regulate the endocytosis of other molecules including Frizzled 3, nephrin, and the matrix metalloproteinase MMP14.
source: Vangl2 has been shown to regulate the endocytosis of other molecules including Frizzled 3 (Shafer et al., 2011), nephrin (Babayeva et al., 2013) or the matrix metalloproteinase MMP14 (Williams et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shafer et al., 2011; Babayeva et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2012.

claim: Vangl2-mediated membrane protein endocytosis might represent an evolutionarily conserved mechanism by which tissue morphogenesis (including neuronal tissue) is controlled in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Therefore, Vangl2-mediated membrane protein endocytosis might represent an evolutionarily conserved mechanism by which tissue morphogenesis (including neuronal tissue) is controlled in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on the data and literature on Vangl2's role in endocytosis.

claim: An increase in axonal growth in vivo could lead the axons to reach the midline too early, before local cues necessary for their crossing are expressed, and as a result the axons would use alternate trajectories that are permissive to their passage.
source: In vivo we could imagine that an increase in axonal growth would lead the axons to reach the midline too early, before local cues necessary for their crossing are expressed, and as a result the axons would use alternate trajectories that are permissive to their passage.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of how the in vitro findings might relate to the in vivo phenotype.

claim: The in vivo phenotype observed in the Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO is more realistically the result of a combination of the disruption of both autonomous and non-autonomous Vangl2-dependant mechanisms.
source: But the in vivo phenotype observed in the Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO is more realistically the result of a combination of the disruption of both autonomous and non-autonomous Vangl2-dependant mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the in vivo phenotype.

claim: Vangl2 is broadly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus early in development and notably at the time of intense neurogenesis.
source: Vangl2 is broadly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus early in development and notably at the time of intense neurogenesis (Tissir and Goffinet, 2006, this manuscript) and its deletion could affect various mechanisms, in neuronal and non-neuronal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tissir and Goffinet, 2006 and data in this manuscript.

claim: The data on the redistribution of Vangl2 at the periphery of the growth cone on the N-cadherin substrate suggest that the composition of the ECM could reciprocally modulate the distribution of Vangl2 molecules in the growth cone and then modulate its behavior.
source: Our data on the redistribution of Vangl2 at the periphery of the growth cone on the N-cadherin substrate suggest that the composition of the ECM could reciprocally modulate the distribution of Vangl2 molecules in the growth cone and then modulate its behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing differential distribution of Vangl2 on N-cadherin vs laminin substrates.

claim: This effect could be mediated via homophilic N-cadherin interactions in trans transmitted via direct or indirect interaction with Vangl2.
source: It seems reasonable to think that this effect could be mediated via homophilic N-cadherin interactions in trans transmitted via direct or indirect interaction with Vangl2.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: In vivo, guidance could be regulated by the interplay between Vangl2 and the ratio of N-cadherin and laminin (ECM composition) present along the growth cone path as it grows.
source: In vivo, we could imagine that guidance is regulated by the interplay between Vangl2 and the ratio of N-cadherin and laminin (ECM composition) present along the growth cone path as it grows.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of how Vangl2 might function in vivo.

claim: Most of the forebrain neurons appear to be able to compensate for the absence of such a Vangl2 control of guidance in vivo.
source: But if this is the case, most of the forebrain neurons appear to be able to compensate for the absence of such a Vangl2 control of guidance in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most commissures appear intact in the Vangl2 cKO mice.

claim: The clear differences in neuronal behavior and in the corresponding in vivo phenotypes, similar for Fzd3 and Celsr3 but different from Vangl2, suggest that the N-cadherin/Vangl2 relationship identified here in hippocampal neurons mostly pertains to outgrowth regulation.
source: Thus, we believe that the clear differences in neuronal behavior and in the corresponding in vivo phenotypes, similar for Fzd3 and Celsr3 but different from Vangl2, suggest that the N-cadherin/Vangl2 relationship identified here in hippocampal neurons mostly pertains to outgrowth regulation (Chai et al., 2014; Hua et al., 2013; Hua et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes and is also supported by citations to Chai et al., 2014; Hua et al., 2013; Hua et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2008.

claim: These results expand a growing body of literature highlighting some links between Vangl2 and components of the ECM during cell migration, notably during convergent extension in the zebrafish.
source: Though mechanistically different, these results expand a growing body of literature highlighting some links between Vangl2 and components of the ECM during cell migration, notably during convergent extension in the zebrafish (Dohn et al., 2013; Jessen and Jessen, 2017; Love et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dohn et al., 2013; Jessen and Jessen, 2017; Love et al., 2018.

claim: In the Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO conditional model, the agenesis of the cc is restricted to the posterior portion which is typical of a developmental deficit, as formation of the cc starts from the anterior part and progresses to the rear.
source: In the Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO conditional model used in this study, the agenesis of the cc is restricted to the posterior portion which is typical of a developmental deficit, as formation of the cc starts from the anterior part and progresses to the rear.
evidence: The claim is based on the observed pattern of corpus callosum agenesis and knowledge of corpus callosum development.

claim: It is suggested that cc crossing may be facilitated by hc in the caudal region.
source: In this same caudal region, it is suggested that cc crossing may be facilitated by hc (Livy and Wahlsten, 1997; Ozaki and Wahlsten, 1992; Wahlsten, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Livy and Wahlsten, 1997; Ozaki and Wahlsten, 1992; Wahlsten, 1981.

claim: In the Vangl2 cKO, the cc deficit is, to a large extent, a secondary consequence of the faulty formation of the hc.
source: Although we cannot exclude that cortical neurons might also react abnormally to the absence of Vangl2, we propose that in the Vangl2 cKO the cc deficit is, to a large extent, a secondary consequence of the faulty formation of the hc.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between the hc and cc deficits.

claim: In the Vangl2 cKO mutant, the cc deficit is not associated with a significant disruption of upper-layer neurons or cortical thickness reduction, as observed in the Loop-tail mouse.
source: In our mutant, the cc deficit is not associated with a significant disruption of upper-layer neurons or cortical thickness reduction, as observed in the Loop-tail mouse (Lake and Sokol, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data showing no change in cortical thickness or Cux1-positive neurons, and is also supported by citation to Lake and Sokol, 2009.

claim: This discrepancy can be partially explained by the absence of severe neural tube defects in the Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO, or in a double Vangl1−/−;Foxg1Cre;Vangl2f/f compound cKO, as compared to mice with germline mutation/deletion such as the Vangl2Lp/Lp mutant or the null Vangl2Δ/Δ mutant.
source: We believe this discrepancy can be partially explained by the absence of severe neural tube defects in the Emx1-Cre*Vangl2 cKO, or in a double Vangl1−/−;Foxg1Cre;Vangl2f/f compound cKO (Qu et al., 2014), as compared to mice with germline mutation/deletion such as the Vangl2Lp/Lp mutant or the null Vangl2Δ/Δ mutant (Song et al., 2010), which present with craniorachischisis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes and is also supported by citations to Qu et al., 2014 and Song et al., 2010.

claim: Some of the central nervous system defects seen in Vangl2Lp/Lp or in Vangl2Δ/Δ embryos brains could be a secondary consequence of the severe disruptions in tissue morphogenesis as observed in these mutants.
source: As such, some of the central nervous system defects seen in Vangl2Lp/Lp or in Vangl2Δ/Δ embryos brains could be a secondary consequence of the severe disruptions in tissue morphogenesis as observed in these mutants.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the phenotypes observed in different Vangl2 mutant models.

claim: A compounding factor in the Vangl2Lp/Lp embryo could be the existence of dominant-negative or gain-of-function properties of the Vangl2Lp protein.
source: Finally, a compounding factor in the Vangl2Lp/Lp embryo could be the existence of dominant-negative or gain-of-function properties of the Vangl2Lp protein, as shown in other systems or suggested in previous studies (Qu et al., 2014; Song et al., 2010; Torban et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Qu et al., 2014; Song et al., 2010; Torban et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2012.

claim: At least some of the severe phenotype in cortical thickness observed by Lake and Sokol are not entirely due to a disruption in the neurogenesis process.
source: It is therefore probable that at least some of the severe phenotype in cortical thickness observed by Lake and Sokol are not entirely due to a disruption in the neurogenesis process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes between different Vangl2 mutant models.

claim: This work offers an original and dynamic view of the role of Vangl2 in neuronal cells and gives insight into how a specific core PCP gene can affect the development and the morphogenesis of neuronal tissue.
source: In summary, this work offers an original and dynamic view of the role of Vangl2 in neuronal cells and gives us insight into how a specific core PCP gene can affects the development and the morphogenesis of neuronal tissue.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the significance of the work.

claim: This is specifically important given the links between core PCP genes and neurodevelopmental or neurological pathologies like neural tube defects and epilepsy.
source: This is specifically important given the links between core PCP genes and neurodevelopmental or neurological pathologies like neural tube defects and epilepsy (Sans et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sans et al., 2016.
